clue.text: I clowned originally in royal house?

definitions.text: I clowned originally in royal house?

indicators.note: in tells us the two opening pieces sit inside the dynastic name

parts.note: York is an English royal house, as in the House of York

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the word clowned

explanation.surface: A jester claims he first played the fool inside a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the jester of Hamlet's Danish court could say 'I clowned' in a royal house.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's dead court jester, whose skull the prince holds, is the clown who could speak these words.

clue.text: Mother-to be seems, to some extent, rather overweight

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A pregnant woman appears to be carrying a little extra weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Being decidedly fat, more than plump, is the dictionary sense of the word.

clue.text: Combine harvester finally brought in by a gent with tie askew

indicators.note: brought in by says the final letter is taken inside the jumbled letters
askew means out of line, so the letters of a gent and tie are set crooked into a new order
finally points to the last letter of the word harvester

explanation.surface: A farm machine's last load is fetched by a man whose necktie is crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Combine harvester' reads as one machine, but 'Combine' alone is the definition. 'askew' rearranges the letters into INTEGATE, and 'brought in by' sets R within it.
explanation.definitionFit: To combine things is to merge or unite them into a single whole, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Martial art demonstrated by artist taken hold of by shrew?

indicators.note: taken hold of by says the artist's letters are gripped within the shrew's name

parts.note: Kate is the shrew of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A painter shows off his self-defence moves while gripped by a small rodent or a nagging woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the shrew is not an animal but Shakespeare's Katherina, called Kate.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese unarmed combat system of strikes and kicks is a well-known fighting discipline.

clue.text: Film luminary was screening finale of Goldfinger

parts.note: a luminary is a celebrated person, a star

indicators.note: screening means hiding behind or around, so the word was encloses the letter
finale of points to the last letter of Goldfinger

explanation.surface: A movie celebrity was showing the climax of a Bond film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screening' suggests cinema but here means concealing: WAS hides R, the last letter of Goldfinger.
explanation.definitionFit: George Lucas's 1977 space opera is one of the best-known movies ever made.

clue.text: Two bears? This is what the highwayman apparently said!

definitions.meaning: to stand is to bear or tolerate, and to deliver is to bear a child, so the two verbs are two senses of bear

definitions.text: This is what the highwayman apparently said
definitions.meaning: the traditional demand of a mounted robber holding up a coach: halt and hand over your valuables

explanation.surface: A riddle asks about two animals, then answers with a robber's catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears' looks like the animals, but it is the verb: two verbs meaning bear, joined by 'and', give the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock command of the eighteenth-century road robber, ordering travellers to stop and give up their money.

clue.text: A female, silver-tongued and wealthy

parts.note: someone silver-tongued speaks smoothly and easily, that is fluently

explanation.surface: A woman described as smooth-talking and rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe people with plenty of money, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: County flags

definitions.meaning: the usual abbreviation of Wiltshire, a county in south-west England
to flag is to droop or lose energy, as a plant does without water

explanation.surface: A shire shows its banners.
explanation.definitionFit: The short form of Wiltshire, an English county, is also a verb meaning droops or tires.

clue.text: As good as gold? Not quite, us!

definitions.text: As good as gold? Not quite, us!

parts.words: As good as gold? Not quite, us!
parts.note: those who finished second and took silver medals speak: nearly as good as the gold winners, but not quite

explanation.walkthrough: 'As good as gold' is the idiom for well-behaved, but here gold is the winner's medal and the speakers are those who just missed it.
explanation.definitionFit: Competitors placed second, who take silver, are the ones who were almost but not quite as good as the winners.

clue.text: Partner improved beer

parts.note: something improved has been made better
a half is a half-pint of beer, as ordered in a British pub

explanation.surface: A spouse brewed a better ale.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'half' is British pub shorthand for half a pint of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular idiom for one's spouse or long-term partner.

clue.text: Good looker that's played by the sea, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for the seaside course is said aloud to give a word that sounds the same

parts.note: links is a seaside golf course, where golf is played on sandy coastal land

explanation.surface: A handsome person is seen at the coast, by report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good looker' suggests an attractive person, but it means something with sharp eyesight.
explanation.definitionFit: This wild cat is proverbially keen-sighted, as in 'lynx-eyed', so it is literally a good looker.

clue.text: Join crew on board, loaded

indicators.note: on board says the crew is placed within the joining word, as people go inside a vessel

parts.note: to wed is to join in marriage
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: Instructions to sign up for a ship's crew that is fully laden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crew' is a rowing eight, which goes 'on board', inside WED.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded and weighted both mean carrying extra heaviness, or biased, as with dice.

clue.text: Lurking in a Parisian area of interest, say

parts.note: un is French for a, as a Parisian would say it

indicators.note: say signals that the word for an area of interest is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: one's scene is one's field of interest, as in 'not my scene'

explanation.surface: Something is hidden in a French zone of curiosity.
explanation.walkthrough: UN is French for 'a'; SCENE, as in 'not my scene', sounds like SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lurking is out of sight and unobserved, so it is not visible.

clue.text: Moon goddess

definitions.meaning: a satellite of Saturn, the planet's second-largest
in Greek myth the Titaness who was mother of Zeus

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like one phrase for a lunar deity such as Selene, but it is two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: One name serves both a satellite of Saturn and the Titan mother of the Olympian gods.

clue.text: Drink after social game

indicators.note: after says the drink comes behind the social gathering in the answer

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance, a social event
Scotch is whisky from Scotland

explanation.surface: Having a drink once the party is over, then a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social' is a noun here: a hop is an informal dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's playground pastime of hopping through chalked squares, one example of a game.

clue.text: Around noon, son seen playing in folly

indicators.note: Around says the jumbled letters go about the letter for midday
playing means fooling about, so the letters of son and seen are rearranged

explanation.surface: At midday a boy is spotted acting the fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges the seven letters into NOSENSE, which goes 'Around' the N for noon, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Folly is foolishness, absurd behaviour or talk, a synonym for rubbish talk.

clue.text: Colour that is raised on blue quilt

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means read upwards, so the colour and the abbreviation are turned round

parts.note: red is a colour
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
down means low in spirits, blue

explanation.surface: A red shade is lifted onto a blue bedcover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns RED + IE into EIDER; 'blue' means sad, DOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed covering stuffed with soft feathers, originally from the eider duck, is a kind of quilt.

clue.text: Poor colt struggling to produce good form

indicators.note: struggling suggests thrashing about, so the letters of poor colt are jumbled

explanation.surface: A weak young horse labours to show good form in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good form' sounds like racing fitness but means correct etiquette.
explanation.definitionFit: Good form is proper conduct, and the official code of correct etiquette has the same meaning.

clue.text: Came out and performed

definitions.meaning: emerged or became visible, as the sun does from behind cloud
took part in a show, as an actor on stage

explanation.surface: Someone emerged and then put on a show.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both emerging into view and taking part in a show or film.

clue.text: Prepare training information

parts.note: to do a dish or room is to prepare it
PE is physical education, school exercise training

explanation.surface: Get ready the coaching data.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prepare' and 'training' read as a sports instruction; PE is physical education.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for inside facts, as in 'give me the dope on him'.

clue.text: Small groom in short horse race

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes
to curry a horse is to groom it with a currycomb

explanation.surface: A little stable lad competes in a brief equine sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'groom' looks like a stable hand but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprint for horses or ponies, in dictionaries a brief dash over a short distance.

clue.text: Confront a leader in council with price

indicators.note: leader in points to the first letter of the word council

parts.note: the cost of a thing is its price

explanation.surface: Challenge a council head about the expense.
explanation.definitionFit: To approach someone boldly and challenge them is the shared sense, a synonym.

clue.text: Ear, perhaps, for a musical instrument

definitions.meaning: the ear is one example of a body part, a part with a specific function
a keyboard instrument with pipes, played in churches

explanation.surface: Using one's hearing to judge something that plays music.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a body part such as the ear and the pipe keyboard instrument.

clue.text: Tear delicate material in front of class

indicators.note: in front of places the fabric before the word for class

parts.note: lace is a fine openwork fabric
a rate is a class or grade, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: Ripping fine fabric in front of a group of pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' could be a drop from the eye; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To lacerate flesh is to rip or gash it, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: A number seem oddly anxious

parts.note: ten is a number

indicators.note: oddly picks the odd-numbered letters, the first and third, of the word seem

explanation.surface: Several people appear strangely nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tense is nervous and on edge, a synonym of worried.

clue.text: Rodgers' last nickname for Hart?

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the name Rodgers

parts.note: a tag is a name or label, a nickname

explanation.surface: Richard Rodgers's final pet name for his lyricist partner Lorenz Hart.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodgers and Hart were a songwriting team, but the hart here is a deer; the question mark signals the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A hart is an adult male red deer, an example of a male deer.

clue.text: Man in the field must have peak on cap

indicators.note: on says the peak follows the cap, joined to it

parts.note: a cover is a cap or lid
a point is a peak or tip

explanation.surface: A cap must have a peak, as a fieldworker's headgear does.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover point is a fielding position in cricket, on the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a fielder stands at named positions, and this is one of them.

clue.text: Dealer caught by officer in charge of dog

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a police dog is worked by its handler

explanation.surface: A trader is arrested by a police dog's minder.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in ship supplies or candles, a trader in particular goods.

clue.text: Rodney at sea, over there

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters of Rodney are muddled

explanation.surface: Admiral Rodney is on the ocean, over there in the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodney suggests the naval admiral, which makes 'at sea' look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned or literary word for at that distant place.
